1850-dover-calais.tagline: One copper wire, wrapped in tree sap, dropped in the Channel.

layers.label: Iron wire armour
layers.note: Ten iron wires laid in a spiral so trawlers and rock could not cut the core.

layers.label: Tarred hemp
layers.note: A cushion between hard armour and soft insulation.

layers.label: Gutta-percha
layers.note: Latex from a Malayan tree — the first plastic that stayed watertight in cold seawater.

layers.label: Copper conductor
layers.note: A single solid copper wire. Every Morse dot crossed the Channel through this.

connectors.label: Brass screw terminal
connectors.note: The wire was simply clamped under a brass screw at the shore station.

1858-transatlantic.tagline: Seven copper strands, 2 500 miles, and about 0.1 words per minute.

layers.label: Iron wire armour
layers.note: 18 iron strands — too light for the job, which is partly why it failed.

layers.label: Tarred hemp
layers.note: Padding and corrosion protection.

layers.label: Gutta-percha
layers.note: Three coats. Any pinhole meant seawater and a dead cable.

layers.label: Stranded copper
layers.note: Seven copper wires twisted together — stranding survives bending better than one thick wire.

connectors.label: Brass screw terminal
connectors.note: Shore ends landed on brass terminals in a wooden testing hut.

1866-transatlantic.tagline: Same idea as 1858, built properly. It lasted decades.

layers.label: Galvanised steel armour
layers.note: Stronger, zinc-coated wires, each wrapped in tarred manila.

layers.label: Jute serving
layers.note: Bedding layer that let the armour flex without biting in.

layers.label: Gutta-percha
layers.note: Four alternating layers of gutta-percha and Chatterton's compound.

layers.label: Stranded copper
layers.note: Heavier copper than 1858 — less resistance, faster signalling.

1876-first-telephone.tagline: Voice, as a wobbling current, on a bare iron line.

layers.label: Cotton braid
layers.note: Waxed cotton — weatherproofing, 1870s style.

layers.label: Rubber insulation
layers.note: Natural rubber kept the line from shorting on wet poles.

layers.label: Iron line wire
layers.note: Iron, not copper — cheap and strong, but lossy and noisy.

connectors.label: Binding post
connectors.note: A screw post on the telephone box; you wrapped the wire round it by hand.

1878-phone-jack.tagline: The plug a telephone operator jammed into a board — still in your guitar amp.

layers.label: Cotton braid
layers.note: Cloth-covered flex, the standard finish before plastics.

layers.label: Rubber insulation
layers.note: Separates the two conductors of the speech circuit.

connectors.label: ¼-inch tip-sleeve plug
connectors.note: Tip carries the signal, sleeve is the return. The shape has not changed in 145 years.

1881-twisted-pair.tagline: Twist the two wires together and the noise cancels itself out.

layers.label: Cotton braid
layers.note: Outer protective braid.

layers.label: Paper insulation
layers.note: Dry paper wrap — cheap, and a fine insulator until it got wet.

1931-coax-patent.tagline: Put the return path *around* the signal and the cable stops radiating.

layers.label: PVC jacket
layers.note: Keeps water and hands off the shield.

layers.label: Copper braid shield
layers.note: The return conductor AND the shield — this is the whole trick of coax.

layers.label: Polyethylene dielectric
layers.note: Holds the centre wire exactly on the axis. Spacing sets the impedance.

layers.label: Copper centre conductor
layers.note: Signal rides here, perfectly surrounded by its own return path.

connectors.label: Coaxial fitting
connectors.note: Early screw fittings kept the shield continuous through the joint.

1936-coax-trials.tagline: 240 telephone calls down one tube of copper.

layers.label: Steel tape armour
layers.note: Long-haul routes were buried; the tape took the abuse.

layers.label: Lead sheath
layers.note: A sealed metal sheath — the only reliable moisture barrier of the era.

layers.label: Copper outer tube
layers.note: A solid copper tube as the return conductor.

layers.label: Disc spacers / air
layers.note: Mostly air, with insulating discs every few centimetres. Air is the best dielectric there is.

layers.label: Copper centre conductor
layers.note: Carried the multiplexed carrier signal.

1954-gotland-hvdc.tagline: Not data — raw power, 98 km under the Baltic.

layers.label: Steel wire armour
layers.note: Double armour against anchors and ice scour.

layers.label: Lead sheath
layers.note: A seamless lead tube — the only thing that reliably keeps seawater out of paper.

layers.label: Oil-impregnated paper
layers.note: Hundreds of paper tapes soaked in insulating oil. Cheap, and it survives 100 kV.

layers.label: Stranded copper conductor
layers.note: Carries 20 MW of direct current to the island of Gotland.

connectors.label: Shore termination
connectors.note: A porcelain bushing the size of a person, transferring the core to the overhead grid.

1950s-xlr.tagline: Three pins that let a microphone run 100 m without picking up a radio station.

layers.label: Braided shield
layers.note: The shield is the third pin — it drains interference to ground.

connectors.label: XLR 3-pin
connectors.note: Pin 1 ground, pins 2 and 3 the balanced pair. Latching, so it cannot fall out mid-show.

1956-tat1.tagline: The first transatlantic telephone cable — with valve amplifiers on the seabed.

layers.label: Steel wire armour
layers.note: Deep-water armour rated for 4 km of ocean.

layers.label: Polyethylene dielectric
layers.note: Polyethylene replaced gutta-percha — stable, low loss, mass-producible.

layers.label: Copper return tube
layers.note: Outer conductor completing the coaxial pair.

layers.label: Copper centre conductor
layers.note: 36 simultaneous telephone calls.

connectors.label: Submerged repeater
connectors.note: Vacuum-tube amplifiers spliced inline every ~70 km, built to run 20 years unattended.

1962-rs232.tagline: One bit at a time, at ±12 volts, and it still runs factory floors.

layers.label: Foil shield
layers.note: Needed because the big voltage swings radiate badly.

connectors.label: DB-25 / DE-9 D-sub
connectors.note: Screw locks on either side, because nobody trusted friction to hold it.

chips.label: Line driver / UART
chips.note: Converts the computer's 5 V logic into the ±12 V swing the standard demands.

1966-fiber-theory.tagline: Kao's insight: the loss wasn't the glass, it was the impurities in it.

layers.label: Acrylate coating
layers.note: Protects the glass surface — a scratch is where a fibre breaks.

layers.label: Cladding glass
layers.note: Slightly lower refractive index, so light striking the boundary reflects back inward.

layers.label: Core glass
layers.note: Ultra-pure silica. Light bounces along inside it by total internal reflection.

connectors.label: Cleaved fibre end
connectors.note: A flat, polished end face — the whole signal enters through this.

1970-centronics.tagline: Eight bits side by side — fast, until the wires started talking to each other.

layers.label: Braided shield
layers.note: 36 wires in a bundle radiate a lot; the braid contained it.

connectors.label: 36-pin Centronics
connectors.note: A wide ribbon connector held on by two spring clips.

1977-first-fiber.tagline: Live phone traffic on light, in Chicago.

layers.label: Aramid yarn
layers.note: Takes the pulling load so the glass never feels the tension.

layers.label: Multimode core
layers.note: A wide core — easy to couple light into, but modes spread the pulse.

connectors.label: SC fibre connector
connectors.note: Spring-loaded ceramic ferrule holds two fibre ends within a micron of each other.

chips.label: LED / photodiode
chips.note: Electricity in, light out at one end; light in, electricity out at the other.

1980-10base5.tagline: The thick yellow hosepipe you drilled into with a 'vampire tap'.

layers.label: PVC jacket
layers.note: Bright yellow by convention, with a black band every 2.5 m marking where you may tap.

layers.label: Foil shield
layers.note: Double shielding — this cable ran through ceilings full of fluorescent lights.

layers.label: Solid copper core
layers.note: The vampire tap's spike bit through everything to reach this.

connectors.label: N-type / vampire tap
connectors.note: A clamp that drove a spike into the core without cutting the cable.

chips.label: Ethernet transceiver (MAU)
chips.note: Bolted onto the tap, it listened for collisions on the shared wire.

1983-midi.tagline: A current loop that let any synth talk to any other — and still does.

layers.label: Braided shield
layers.note: Connected at one end only, to stop ground loops humming through the PA.

connectors.label: 5-pin DIN
connectors.note: Only three pins are used. The other two were left for a future that never came.

chips.label: Opto-isolator
chips.note: Light, not wire, carries the signal across the gap — so two amps never share a ground.

1985-10base2.tagline: Cheapernet: thin coax, BNC twists, and one loose end killing the whole office.

layers.label: Polyethylene dielectric
layers.note: 50 Ω — thinner and far more flexible than 10BASE5.

connectors.label: BNC T-connector
connectors.note: A quarter turn to lock. Every machine sat on the same wire, so one bad terminator downed the segment.

1985-token-ring.tagline: IBM's orderly answer to Ethernet: you may only speak while holding the token.

layers.label: Overall braid
layers.note: IBM Type 1 was fully shielded — heavy, expensive, and very quiet electrically.

connectors.label: IBM Data Connector
connectors.note: A hermaphroditic connector — any plug mates with any other, no male or female.

chips.label: Ring interface chip
chips.note: Repeats every frame around the ring and strips its own messages back off.

1986-scsi.tagline: Fast, capable, and cursed with termination problems and ID conflicts.

connectors.label: Centronics-50 / DB-25
connectors.note: Every device needed a unique ID, and the last one on the chain needed a terminator.

chips.label: SCSI controller
chips.note: Arbitrates which of up to eight devices may drive the shared bus.

1988-tat8.tagline: The Atlantic goes optical: 40 000 calls at once.

layers.label: Steel wire strength member
layers.note: Takes the weight of the cable hanging off the back of the ship.

layers.label: Copper power conductor
layers.note: Carries DC power to the optical repeaters on the seabed.

layers.label: Filling gel
layers.note: Blocks water from running along inside the tube if the sheath is breached.

layers.label: Fibre pairs
layers.note: Three working pairs of single-mode fibre.

connectors.label: Optical repeater
connectors.note: Regenerated the light pulses every ~70 km along the ocean floor.

chips.label: Laser + regenerator
chips.note: Converted light to electrical bits and back to clean light.

1986-ide-ata.tagline: The grey ribbon inside every beige PC — 40 wires, one red stripe.

layers.label: PVC ribbon
layers.note: Flat, unshielded, and colour-coded by a single red stripe marking pin 1.

connectors.label: 40-pin IDC header
connectors.note: Insulation-displacement: the connector's blades slice straight through the ribbon.

chips.label: Drive controller
chips.note: IDE's trick was moving the controller onto the drive itself — Integrated Drive Electronics.

1987-vga.tagline: Three analogue colour signals, each in its own miniature coax.

connectors.label: DE-15 (VGA)
connectors.note: 15 pins in three rows, with thumbscrews. Purely analogue — the monitor never knew what pixels were.

chips.label: RAMDAC
chips.note: Converts the digital framebuffer into three smooth analogue voltages, millions of times a second.

1990-10baset.tagline: Ethernet leaves the thick yellow coax and moves onto phone-style wire.

layers.label: PVC jacket
layers.note: Four pairs in one sheath — the shape office cabling took for the next 30 years.

connectors.label: RJ45 (8P8C)
connectors.note: Eight gold-plated contacts that pierce the wire insulation when crimped.

chips.label: Ethernet PHY
chips.note: Turns bits into the precise voltage waveform the pairs carry.

1987-ps2.tagline: Purple for keyboard, green for mouse — and never hot-pluggable.

connectors.label: 6-pin mini-DIN
connectors.note: Keyed so it only goes in one way — which you discovered by feel, under a desk.

chips.label: Keyboard controller
chips.note: Scans the key matrix and clocks each keypress out one bit at a time.

1991-568-cat5.tagline: One standard socket for any building, any vendor.

layers.label: Rip cord + separator
layers.note: The string you pull to split the jacket without nicking the pairs.

connectors.label: RJ45 (8P8C)
connectors.note: The standard that made structured cabling interchangeable.

1995-fast-ethernet.tagline: Ten times faster on the same four pairs — by twisting tighter.

layers.label: Pair separator
layers.note: Each pair gets a different twist rate so neighbours do not couple.

chips.label: 100BASE-TX PHY
chips.note: Encodes data so the signal stays inside the cable's bandwidth.

1995-firewire.tagline: Faster than USB, and devices could talk to each other without a PC.

connectors.label: IEEE 1394 6-pin
connectors.note: Carried bus power, so a camcorder could run off the cable.

chips.label: 1394 link/PHY
chips.note: Every device is a peer with its own bus arbitration — no host computer required.

1996-usb1.tagline: One connector to replace serial, parallel, PS/2 and the rest.

layers.label: Braided shield
layers.note: Keeps USB's fast edges from radiating into your radio.

layers.label: Aluminium foil
layers.note: Foil catches the high frequencies the braid misses.

connectors.label: USB Type-A
connectors.note: Deliberately un-reversible — and famously hard to insert first try.

chips.label: USB controller
chips.note: Handles enumeration: the handshake where your PC asks 'what are you?'

1997-docsis1.tagline: The TV cable learns to talk back.

layers.label: Braided shield
layers.note: 60 % coverage braid over the foil.

layers.label: Aluminium foil
layers.note: Bonded foil — the primary shield against ingress.

layers.label: Foamed polyethylene
layers.note: Mostly gas bubbles: lower loss than solid plastic.

layers.label: Copper-clad steel core
layers.note: Steel for strength, copper skin because RF only travels on the surface.

connectors.label: F-type screw connector
connectors.note: The centre conductor of the cable *is* the connector pin — no separate pin needed.

chips.label: DOCSIS modem SoC
chips.note: Tunes RF channels and turns them into IP packets.

1999-dvi.tagline: The bridge cable: digital pins and analogue pins in one shell.

connectors.label: DVI-I dual link
connectors.note: 24 digital pins plus 4 analogue ones, so it could drive a VGA monitor through an adapter.

chips.label: TMDS transmitter
chips.note: The same signalling HDMI would adopt three years later.

2002-hdmi1.tagline: Video, audio and control down one plug.

layers.label: Overall braid
layers.note: A second shield around the whole bundle.

connectors.label: HDMI Type-A
connectors.note: 19 pins: three video pairs, a clock, and a control channel.

chips.label: TMDS transmitter
chips.note: Serialises each colour channel and scrambles it to keep the signal balanced.

2002-cat6.tagline: A plastic spine down the middle to keep the four pairs apart.

layers.label: Cross-filler spine
layers.note: An X-shaped plastic spline holding each pair in its own quadrant — the visual signature of Cat6.

chips.label: Gigabit PHY
chips.note: Runs all four pairs at once, in both directions simultaneously, and cancels its own echo.

2003-sata.tagline: Seven wires beat forty: serial won because parallel ran out of road.

layers.label: Foil + drain
layers.note: Each pair individually wrapped — at 6 GHz the pairs must not hear each other.

connectors.label: SATA 7-pin
connectors.note: L-shaped so it only fits one way. Three grounds separate the two pairs.

chips.label: SATA PHY
chips.note: Serialises at 6 GHz — far past the point where 40 parallel wires could stay in step.

2003-poe.tagline: One cable that carries the network *and* runs the device off it.

connectors.label: RJ45 (8P8C)
connectors.note: Identical plug to plain Ethernet — the power is negotiated, not wired in.

chips.label: PoE controller (PSE/PD)
chips.note: The switch probes for a known resistance before it dares apply 48 V, so it never fries a laptop.

2006-displayport.tagline: Video as data packets, not as a scanning beam.

connectors.label: DisplayPort
connectors.note: A latching plug — squeeze the release or you will pull your monitor off the desk.

chips.label: DisplayPort transmitter
chips.note: Chops the image into micro-packets, so one cable can drive several monitors in a chain.

2006-10gbase-t.tagline: Ten gigabits over twisted copper — an idea most engineers called impossible.

layers.label: Overall braid
layers.note: Cat6a adds shielding to fight alien crosstalk — interference from the cable lying next to it.

chips.label: 10GBASE-T DSP
chips.note: Burns several watts running error correction and echo cancellation just to keep the link alive.

2008-usb3.tagline: Two extra shielded pairs bolted onto USB 2.0, one each way.

connectors.label: USB 3.0 Type-A
connectors.note: Five extra contacts set deeper in the shell — which is why the plug is blue.

chips.label: SuperSpeed PHY
chips.note: Recovers a 5 GHz clock from the data stream itself.

2011-thunderbolt.tagline: PCI Express, stretched down a cable — your GPU on the end of a wire.

connectors.label: Thunderbolt (USB-C shell)
connectors.note: Same plug as USB-C, but only certified cables carry the full 40 Gb/s.

chips.label: Thunderbolt retimer
chips.note: An active chip in each plug that receives the signal, cleans it, and re-sends it — without it the cable could only be a few centimetres long.

chips.label: E-marker IC
chips.note: Tells the host this is a 40 Gb/s cable and not a charging lead.

2012-lightning.tagline: The first reversible phone plug — with a chip that decides what each pin does.

connectors.label: Lightning 8-pin
connectors.note: Reversible because the plug's chip re-assigns the pins depending on which way up it went in.

chips.label: Authentication IC
chips.note: Apple's MFi chip. If it is missing or cloned, the phone refuses the cable — the reason third-party leads suddenly stopped working after updates.

2014-usbc.tagline: Reversible, 100 W capable — and the first cable with a brain inside the plug.

connectors.label: USB Type-C
connectors.note: 24 contacts, mirrored top and bottom, so it works either way up.

chips.label: E-marker IC
chips.note: A real chip moulded into the plug. The charger asks it how much current the cable can survive — that is why a cheap cable charges your laptop slowly.

chips.label: Retimer
chips.note: In long high-speed cables, it cleans up and re-transmits the signal mid-flight.

2017-8023bs.tagline: Eight fibres in parallel, 50 Gb/s on each.

layers.label: LSZH jacket
layers.note: Low-smoke zero-halogen — it will not poison a data hall if it burns.

layers.label: Ribbon matrix
layers.note: Fibres bonded side by side in a flat ribbon so all eight terminate at once.

connectors.label: MPO/MTP ribbon connector
connectors.note: Twelve fibres land in one push-on ferrule, aligned by two steel guide pins.

chips.label: DSP + optical engine
chips.note: A digital signal processor drives eight lasers and un-smears what comes back.

2019-usb4.tagline: One cable that carries USB, DisplayPort and PCIe at the same time, in shares.

chips.label: USB4 router
chips.note: Splits the cable's bandwidth on the fly — give the monitor more, the SSD gets less.

chips.label: E-marker IC
chips.note: Declares speed and wattage so the host knows what the cable can actually do.

2020-800g.tagline: Colour, phase and polarisation all carry data at once.

layers.label: Single-mode core
layers.note: Only ~9 µm across — narrow enough that light travels one single path.

connectors.label: LC duplex connector
connectors.note: A latching ceramic ferrule; one fibre out, one fibre back.

chips.label: Coherent DSP
chips.note: Measures the light's phase and polarisation, then undoes the distortion of 1 000 km of glass — billions of operations per second.

2024-eu-usbc.tagline: One charger for everything, by law.

connectors.label: USB Type-C
connectors.note: The connector the EU made mandatory for phones, tablets and cameras.

chips.label: E-marker IC
chips.note: Declares the cable's wattage and speed rating. Required for anything above 60 W.

2020s-self-healing.tagline: Cut it, and the insulation grows back.

layers.label: Microcapsule layer
layers.note: Tiny capsules of healing agent. A tear ruptures them and the liquid floods the gap and sets.

layers.label: Self-healing polymer
layers.note: Reversible bonds re-form across a cut when the two faces touch again.

layers.label: Conductive core
layers.note: Some designs use a liquid-metal core that simply flows back together.

chips.label: Health-monitor IC
chips.note: Watches resistance along the cable and reports damage before the link drops.
